title: An RPZ backflow preventer uses two checks and a relief zone you must not obstruct
description: Identify the reduced pressure zone assembly, understand relief discharge, testing, hazard use, drainage, and the repair-versus-replacement path.
prompt: What is happening at the RPZ?
answer: An RPZ is a testable assembly that protects against backsiphonage and backpressure for applicable hazards. Its relief valve is a safety function and can discharge when pressure relationships or internal components are wrong.
urgency: Never plug the relief opening. Indoor installations need drainage sized for potential discharge according to the model and local requirements.
diagramAlt: RPZ backflow assembly with first check, reduced pressure zone, relief valve, and second check
identifiers: Two checks surround a lower-pressure zone.
A relief valve opens from the zone to atmosphere.
Shutoffs and test cocks allow field testing.

choices.label: Relief valve is discharging
choices.detail: Use the vent-discharge diagnostic and keep it open.

choices.label: The assembly failed a test
choices.detail: Move through repair, retest, and accepted submission.

choices.label: I need to identify or replace it
choices.detail: Record the model, size, approval, and installation footprint.

steps.title: Identify the full assembly
steps.body: Record manufacturer, model, size, orientation, and approval label.

steps.title: Protect the relief path
steps.body: Keep drainage and air space unobstructed.

steps.title: Use the local test workflow
steps.body: Eligibility, frequency, repair, retest, and submission come from the utility.

safeChecks: Photograph the relief opening and drain.
Keep the test report and notice.
notThisDevice: A PVB protects only against applicable backsiphonage conditions.
A DCVA has no relief zone.
A regulator controls pressure rather than cross-connection risk.
evidenceNote: The exact listing, manufacturer manual, hazard classification, and local authority determine RPZ application and testing.
